top.line: How technical debt stalled the Open Security Summit, what the code shows, and why to restart it now.
top.para: The summit treated every participant as a presenter, and in 2018 its website was edited by 180 people. Each year's site was copied from the last with more exceptions and no refactoring; the templates froze in 2022 while content kept coming, and contributors fell to 14. The follow-up never scaled. Agents can now map, personalise and follow up. It needs funding.

in-short.line: Seven lines: participants as presenters, the website, the debt, the freeze, the people, the follow-up, the restart.
in-short.para: The model was every participant a presenter, and the website was part of it, with 180 committers in 2018. Each year copied the last; the code froze in 2022 at about 9,600 template lines; committers fell to 14 by 2024; the follow-up never scaled. Restart with agents, in London, online and for hosted projects, with funding.

history.line: From the OWASP Summits of 2008, 2011 and 2017 to the Open Security Summit and its mini-summits.
history.para: After the Algarve, Lisbon and Woburn summits came the Open Security Summit: Woburn, 4 to 8 June 2018; England, 3 to 7 June 2019; fully online, 15 to 19 June 2020; then monthly online mini-summits from October 2020 to September 2024. A CIC since April 2019, now proposed as the home of Agent Behaviour Policies.

website.line: The website was part of the summit: participants edited their own pages and sessions.
website.para: A Hugo site in a public repository, where participants kept their pages, sessions and outcomes. 180 people committed in 2018, 434 commits on the summit's first day, and nearly 600 on 2 and 3 June 2019. In a couple of summits we nailed the structure: participants, sessions, tracks, schedules and outcomes as linked files.

code.line: The repositories show the debt: copies of copies, growing templates, frozen code, leftovers.
code.para: Four site repositories hold 19,045 commits. Most template files were copied year to year. Templates grew from about 5,200 to 9,600 lines, conditions from 255 to 408, partials from 110 to 218, then stopped changing in 2022 while content went from 140 to 998 files. Year-specific exceptions, stale pages and a re-pinned Hugo version show the drift.

people.line: The people went: from 180 committing in 2018 to 14 in 2024, and the live site stopped in 2024.
people.para: Commits stayed high through 2022 and 2023 but from fewer people, as the site became something a few maintained rather than something participants changed. The live home page still announces the next summit for December 2024; the last real work was that month.

follow-up.line: The material is there, 409 session pages and 194 recordings; the follow-up never scaled.
follow-up.para: Working sessions on application security, threat modelling, DevSecOps, governance and AI hold a lot of knowledge, some of my own history among it, and much of it got lost. Online, we could run sessions but not afford a personal path and follow-up for each participant, the same pattern as the jobs that never scaled.

now.line: Restart with agents: map the data, analyse the videos, personalise, follow up; then London, online and hosted projects.
now.para: Not by rebuilding the site first: an agent maps everything, connects the dots, analyses what was said, and creates personal pages and follow-up. Then real events in London, shorter online sessions with more people, and a home for open source projects, starting with Agent Behaviour Policies. It needs somebody to fund it.

lesson.line: Technical debt without a team to pay it down arrives as friction, not a break.
lesson.para: Each summit added a little and each exception made sense, and the cost came as slower changes, fewer contributors and follow-up that never happened. The potential was there all along; the debt and the cost of follow-up kept it from being reached.

limits.line: Counts from public repositories; people by email; dead partials a sign; plans need funding.
limits.para: The counts are from the public repositories, all branches, on 21 October 2026. People are counted by email address, so one person with two counts twice. Partials not called by name may be called another way. Hosting projects is a proposal, and the London events and online sessions need funding.

sources.line: A voice memo, the four summit repositories, the live site, and the history on diniscruz.ai.
sources.para: A voice memo of 21 October 2026; the git history and files of oss2018, oss2019, oss2020 and oss-website and the OpenSecuritySummit organisation on GitHub; the live summit site; the history of the OWASP in-person summits on diniscruz.ai; and related newsroom articles.
